podcast.body: A song recorded in 1968 that features four minutes of the vocable "na na na na." At 26 years old, McCartney was able to take his tenor range to a very high F for this song. "if we go back to 1968 and the recording of Hey Jude, a song that features four minutes of the vocal ball, na na na na, McCartney takes his tenor range to a very high F."

podcast.body: Approximately two minutes and 57 seconds into "Hey Jude," a "bum note" was struck, followed by an unintelligible utterance in the mix. Those present at the recording claim it was John Lennon or Paul McCartney saying "F-ing hell," marking it as another alleged instance of an unintentional F-bomb on record. "Someone, maybe John, maybe Paul, hits a bum note at about two minutes and 57 seconds into the song."

podcast.body: In the late summer of 1968, "Hey Jude" debuted on the Hot 100 at number ten, setting a new record for the chart's highest debut ever. This was a significant achievement for The Beatles in the analog era, where high debuts were rare due to manual data collection and the Hot 100's unique blend of sales and airplay. "the Beatles debuted on the Hot 100 all the way up at number ten with Hey Jude, a new record for the charts highest debut ever."

podcast.body: Paul McCartney wrote "Hey Jude" as a song of comfort for John Lennon's son, Julian. This seven-minute epic became the Beatles' single with the most weeks at number one. "Hey Jude, Paul McCartney's song of comfort for John Lennon's son, Julian."

srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

podcast.body: Paul McCartney's seven-minute epic song of comfort for John Lennon's son, Julian, spent nine weeks at number one, the most for any Beatles single. It ruled the chart from September through November 1968, impressively taking the year-end title despite its late-year dominance. The Beatles were one of only two officially named artists to score the Hot 100 Year End number one twice, the other being George Michael. "Hey Jude, Paul McCartney's song of comfort for John Lennon's son, Julian, racked up the most weeks on top of any Beatles single."

podcast.body: Released as a prominent A-side, "Hey Jude" was backed with a fast version of "Revolution." This pairing highlights the band's practice of releasing strong, noteworthy tracks on both sides of their singles. "Hey Jude, on the A side, came with the fast version of Revolution on the B side."

podcast.body: This seven-minute song, released in 1968, was a number one hit and notably longer than the typical five-minute ideal length for one side of a 45 RPM vinyl single. Its length was an exception to the standard format that had largely dictated popular song duration since the 1940s. "a few hits like the Beatles seven minute 1968 number one, Hey Jude, were longer."

podcast.body: This song is mentioned in the context of Arkells' song "John Lennon," where a character mistakenly describes "Hey Jude" as an obscure song that followed her around Europe, despite it being "the most popular song of all time." "It was hajued by the Beatles. I was like, that's the most popular song of all time."

podcast.body: This song is noted for its extensive coda, which extends for three and a half to four minutes. Its long fade-out exemplifies the band's adoption of fade-out techniques after they ceased touring in 1966 and became primarily a studio band, no longer needing to provide proper endings for live performances. "And I point to Hey Jude as an example and the Coda that takes three and a half minutes, four minutes to wind down."

podcast.body: This song's style of building and building was consciously borrowed by Barry Manilow for his song "Could It Be Magic" to create a "musical orgasm." "Barry then borrowed the style of Hay Jude by the Beatles because I shall directly quote, it should build and build until you think you can't take it anymore. It should be a musical orgasm."
